extracted.intended_audience: computational linguists, NLP researchers, and practitioners building or evaluating sentiment lexicons
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and evaluation criteria for building and testing sentiment/semantic-orientation (SO) lexicons, including Mechanical Turk annotation protocols, expected response distributions, agreement metrics, dictionary-to-SO mapping, and use within the SO-CAL system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical Turk worker qualification and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict tasks to Turkers with extremely high approval rating (99%); request Turkers with specific qualifications or high approval ratings; requesters may reject incorrect work which lowers approval rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping the task simple is important; quality is controlled through Turker qualifications/approval ratings; reject incorrect work; ensure no Turker answers the same question twice. Early testing suggested results were mostly acceptable when restricted to 99% approval Turkers, though some noise from anonymous Turkers is inherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No repeated responses by same Turker
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that no Turker provided an answer to the same question twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although each set included work by multiple Turkers (so 6 sets ≠ six annotators), forbidding duplicate Turker responses per question increases diversity of responses and is considered positive for the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum corpus frequency for inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: When filtering candidate lexicon words, include a word in analysis only if it appeared at least five times in both large corpora used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to adjective dictionary (resulting in 483 adjectives); excludes low-frequency words to focus evaluation on commonly occurring items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude multi-word expressions and ambiguous senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with full dictionary but remove multi-word expressions and words with ambiguous or context-dependent sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually created dictionaries tended to exclude ambiguous words or words that convey sentiment only in some occasions; such exclusions improve performance by reducing noise from word-sense ambiguity and POS errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-way single-word identification task
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators decide whether a single word is positive, negative, or neutral (three-way decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simpler task avoids forcing Turkers to use the 11-point SO scale, making the task less onerous and less subject to individual bias. For this task the study sampled 400 adjectives and solicited six judgments per word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise word comparison task (same-polarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present pairs of polar words (positive vs positive, negative vs negative) and ask whether one is stronger, the other stronger, or they are the same strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Created 500 positive pairs and 500 negative pairs; for each pair solicited six judgments. Segregate by polarity, randomly select first by SO then by word, lower probability of picking high absolute SO words, discount recently-used words, explicitly disallow duplicate pairs to avoid repetition effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation evaluation task (negated vs opposite polarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare negated words to words of opposite polarity (e.g., 'not bad' vs 'good') to test negation models (switch vs shift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary goal is to evaluate correspondence of negation models to human intuition across many cases; the study created four data sets comparing negated words to opposite polarity words and assumed the dictionary is generally correct, using post-negation SO values as input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensifier (adverbial modifier) pairwise comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare pairs of adverbial intensifiers for relative strength using a uniform adjective pairing to assist Turkers (e.g., 'very' + likeable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selected 500 pairs of adverbial modifiers, randomly selecting first by modifier value then by word, discounting pairs if words appeared in recent pairs. Consider splitting intensifiers into downplayers vs ampliﬁers to reduce noise and ambiguity (comparative/pragmatic intensifiers can be hard to interpret outside discourse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicted distributional characteristics for a good SO ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: A good ranking should show that (1) percentage of 'equal/neutral' judgments is maximized at the expected SO point and polar responses are relatively balanced; (2) as SO moves away from 0, expect a linear increase in the appropriate polar response with a corresponding drop in other responses; (3) polar responses may hit a maximum and then plateau (may not reach 100% due to noise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are formal expectations used to validate dictionaries using the single-word and pairwise tasks; deviations can indicate scale non-linearity, problematic categories, or noise at spectrum edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple annotators and compute average pairwise agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicit multiple judgments per item (six in this study) and calculate average percentage of pairwise agreement (number of agreeing Turker pairs divided by total possible pairings) to assess correspondence patterns across SO values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret pairwise agreement as reflecting the SO scale rather than traditional inter-annotator reliability—disagreement is expected and informative (e.g., agreement 60.1% for ±1 words vs 98.2% for ±5 words). Note pairwise agreement drops non-linearly with each dissenting annotator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret disagreement as signal for scale granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: High disagreement at low absolute SO values (e.g., 1/−1) suggests these cases may be inherently ambiguous or the scale is too coarse/fine for reliable discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Turkers largely agree on extreme SO words but disagree on near-neutral ones, this pattern reflects the underlying semantic orientation scale rather than annotator error; use such patterns to refine the dictionary or scale granularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling strategy to ensure coverage across SO spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: For single-word tasks sample first by SO (ensuring neutral words included) then by word; for pairwise tasks sample by SO difference and control for overrepresentation of high-absolute-SO words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pure random sampling which under-samples extremes; re-sample if the word was used before; discount words used recently; explicitly disallow duplicate pairs to avoid repeated high-frequency items.

rubrics_metrics.name: MT correspondence metric for dictionary evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: MT correspondence = (Mechanical Turk judgments predicted by dictionary) / (Total Mechanical Turk judgments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MT correspondence as a relative measure to compare how well different dictionaries predict human judgments. Be aware of upper bounds less than 100% due to annotator disagreement (e.g., single-word highest possible MT correspondence 79%; negative adjective task highest 76.8%). Partial matches (e.g., one rater thinks A>B and another thinks A=B) can count as fractional correspondence (50%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bucket design for mapping continuous SO values to discrete categories
rubrics_metrics.description: When converting continuous SO scores to discrete buckets (to compare with human three-way/11-point judgments), choose bucket sizes thoughtfully (e.g., used a neutral (zero) bucket twice the size of other buckets for single-word tasks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bucket choice affects MT correspondence; increasing number of buckets can boost correspondence for some dictionaries but may interact with underuse of 'same' judgments—interpret results accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping coarse/binary lexicons to SO scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert dictionaries lacking fine-grained SO values by assigning representative SO numbers (examples: Maryland dictionary assigned +3 to positive and −3 to negative; Subjectivity weak→±2, strong→±4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose mapping values to fit the SO-CAL scale and be consistent across comparisons; mapping choices influence downstream performance and may require domain-specific adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: SentiWordNet SO calculation options
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methods: first-sense method SO(w) = 5 × (Pos(f) − Neg(f)) where f is first sense; average-across-senses method SO(w) = (5/|senses|) × sum_{x in senses} (Pos(x) − Neg(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different versions and methods (SentiWordNet 1.0 vs 3.0; first-sense vs average) perform differently under Basic vs Full SO-CAL settings; choose method aware of domain positive-bias and intended SO-CAL feature use.

rubrics_metrics.name: SO-CAL feature modes: Basic vs Full
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic mode sums SO values of words in text with no linguistic features; Full mode enables SO-CAL features including intensification and negation handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full (with features) generally improves performance across dictionaries and corpora (statistically significant improvements), but benefit magnitude depends on dictionary reliability and domain; disable negative weighting for dictionaries/domains where it causes degradation (e.g., Maryland dictionary in movie reviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative weighting and domain-specific adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply negative weighting to counter positive bias in some lexicons, but disable or tune this for domains where negative weighting is inappropriate (e.g., movie reviews where negative terms are more prevalent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: disabled negative weighting for Maryland dictionary because it contained disproportionately many negative words; adjustments can materially affect movie-domain performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical testing for dictionary comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing performance across dictionaries and settings, test for statistical significance (e.g., report p < 0.05 for improvements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports SO-CAL dictionary performance is significantly better than alternatives (p < 0.05); include such testing when claiming superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-expansion of lexicons; prefer judicious restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding more words to a dictionary can add noise (due to word-sense ambiguity, POS tagging errors, or low strength) and may not improve performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude neutral words and many mild-orientation words to focus on stronger sentiment-bearing terms; manual curation that excludes ambiguous/rarely-sentimental words tends to yield superior lexicons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling poor annotators and sabotage
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify Turkers with below-chance agreement or anomalous patterns (e.g., a single Turker supplying many low-quality responses) and remove their data; re-solicit replacements where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual inspection and agreement statistics can reveal problematic Turkers; removing such data can materially raise pairwise agreement on tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'same' underuse and scale granularity trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Turkers underuse the 'same' (equal) designation in pairwise tasks; this may reflect scale coarseness or genuine difficulty comparing words that differ in application (domain/context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off: making scale finer (more SO values) could increase ranker difficulty and not yield benefits; instead use current scale and use data to identify problematic words for manual refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of uniform context to evaluate modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating intensifiers, present them with a uniform adjective (e.g., 'likeable') to assist Turkers in interpreting relative strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces variability due to adjective selection; nonetheless, comparative/pragmatic intensifiers (more, less, hardly) can still be difficult to interpret out of discourse context and produce noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-aware lexicon coverage considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious of lexicons that have excessive coverage (e.g., Maryland, SentiWordNet/WordNet-derived) because they may tag many non-sentiment-bearing words, reducing precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage without POS classification or sense disambiguation leads to false positives (e.g., 'plot' as negative because verb sense is negative). Manually curated lexicons with targeted coverage often perform better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evaluation corpora and task alignment (polarity identification accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate lexicons by running them within an application (e.g., SO-CAL) on labeled corpora and reporting percent correct for polarity identification (deciding whether a text is negative or positive) across multiple corpora/domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report per-corpus and overall accuracy; compare Basic vs Full features; be aware that domain characteristics (positive/negative bias) can change relative performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect asymmetry between positive and negative judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutral words are sometimes interpreted as positive but almost never as negative, reflecting a default positive bias and the marked nature of negative expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for this asymmetry when interpreting curves and designing weighting or post-processing; this observation also impacts predictions for negation and dictionary correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of negation models using human data
rubrics_metrics.description: Use MT judgments to compare simplistic negation models (switch vs shift); measure correspondence (e.g., shift model accounted for 45.2% of MT judgments, switch for 33.4%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negation is more complicated than either model fully captures; empirical correspondence helps decide which model better captures general trends, but neither is conclusive.
